description: Decision patterns for feature scaling and normalization

patterns.name: Standard Scaling - Normal Distribution
patterns.condition: Features approximately normally distributed AND no significant outliers
patterns.explanation: StandardScaler transforms features to have mean=0 and std=1. Ideal for normally distributed features without extreme outliers.
patterns.pitfalls: Sensitive to outliers — a single extreme value can shift mean/std and compress the majority of data.
patterns.example: Applied StandardScaler to 'age' and 'income' — both approximately normal, no extreme outliers detected.

patterns.name: Robust Scaling - Outliers Present
patterns.condition: Features have significant outliers OR skewed distributions
patterns.explanation: Uses median and interquartile range instead of mean and std. Not influenced by extreme values. The gold standard when outliers are present.
patterns.pitfalls: Resulting features may not have 0 mean or unit variance, which some algorithms may expect.
patterns.example: Applied RobustScaler because extreme outliers detected in salary column (99th percentile: $450K vs median: $62K).

patterns.name: MinMax Scaling - Bounded Range Needed
patterns.condition: Features need to be in a specific range (0 to 1) OR data has no significant outliers
patterns.explanation: Squeezes all values into [0, 1] range. Preserves the shape of the original distribution. Ideal when the algorithm requires bounded inputs.
patterns.pitfalls: Extremely sensitive to outliers — one extreme value compresses all other values into a tiny range.
patterns.example: Applied MinMaxScaler to pixel values and percentage features — these have natural [0, 255] and [0, 100] bounds.

patterns.name: No Scaling Needed - Tree Models
patterns.condition: Downstream model is tree-based (Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost)
patterns.explanation: Tree-based models make decisions at split points (thresholds). They are completely scale-invariant — multiplying a feature by 1000 doesn't change the splits.
patterns.pitfalls: Adding scaling is harmless but wasteful. It adds unnecessary computation and complexity.
patterns.example: No scaling applied — preparing data for XGBoost classifier, which is scale-invariant.

patterns.name: Log Transformation - Heavily Skewed
patterns.condition: Feature is heavily right-skewed (skewness > 2) with all positive values
patterns.explanation: Log transformation compresses the range of large values and spreads out small values, making the distribution more normal. The +1 handles zero values.
patterns.pitfalls: Cannot handle negative values. Using log(x+1) to handle zeros. Check that transformation actually reduces skewness.
patterns.example: Applied log(x+1) transform to 'annual_revenue' — skewness reduced from 4.2 to 0.3, making the distribution suitable for linear models.

patterns.name: Power Transformation - Moderate Skew
patterns.explanation: Box-Cox (positive values only) and Yeo-Johnson (handles negatives) find the optimal power to transform the data toward normality.
best_for: Features that need normalization but aren't heavily skewed
patterns.pitfalls: Box-Cox requires strictly positive values. Yeo-Johnson is more flexible. The optimal lambda may vary between train/test.
patterns.example: Applied Yeo-Johnson power transform to 'transaction_amount' — skewness reduced from 1.4 to 0.08.

decision_tree: 1. Is the model tree-based? → No scaling needed
3. Is the distribution heavily right-skewed (skew > 2, positive values)? → Log transform
4. Is the distribution moderately skewed? → Power transform (Yeo-Johnson)
5. Is the distribution approximately normal? → StandardScaler
6. Does the algorithm need bounded [0,1] inputs? → MinMaxScaler
7. Default for neural networks? → StandardScaler or MinMaxScaler
